title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
directAnswer: Store words in a trie exactly like Implement Trie. `addWord` is the standard insert. `search` is a DFS over the trie: on a normal letter follow that one child; on a `.` wildcard recurse into EVERY existing child. A match means the DFS reaches the end of the pattern at a node whose `isEnd` is true.

remember.pattern: Trie + DFS backtracking to handle '.' wildcards
rules: A `.` matches any single character → recurse into **every** child of the current node.
A normal letter follows **exactly one** child; bail out (return false) if that child is missing.
The base case (pattern exhausted) returns **node.isEnd**, not just true — the path must end on a real word.
Pass the **node + index** down the recursion; don't slice the string repeatedly.
Return **as soon as any branch matches** (`any(...)`) — don't keep searching once one path succeeds.
whenToUse: Exact-match dictionary plus single-character wildcards in queries
Pattern matching where '.' (or '?') stands for 'any one character'
You already reach for a trie, and queries are partly unknown
Regex-lite matching over a fixed word set
antiSignals: No wildcards → a plain HashSet / Trie search is enough
Wildcards can match MANY characters ('*') → this is full regex / DP, not a single-step branch
Only one word ever stored → DFS over a trie is overkill
Patterns are mostly dots → DFS fans out to O(26^L); consider constraints carefully
remember.takeaway: The wildcard is the whole problem: a literal letter prunes to one child, a dot forces you to branch over all children and backtrack. It's the canonical 'trie + DFS' marriage — once you can write this search, Word Search II's grid DFS over a trie feels like the same move.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can extend a known structure (the trie) with a recursive search that backtracks. The dot wildcard is a deliberate fork-in-the-road that converts an iterative walk into a DFS.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Treating search iteratively and getting stuck on the dot (you can't pick one child), or returning true at the end of the pattern without checking isEnd (so a prefix wrongly matches).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Recognise instantly that '.' turns the walk into DFS-with-backtracking, pass node+index instead of slicing strings, short-circuit on the first matching branch, and discuss that an all-dots query can blow up to O(26^L).

problemStatement:
Design a data structure that supports adding new words and finding if a string matches any previously added string.

Implement the `WordDictionary` class:

- `WordDictionary()` initializes the object.
- `void addWord(word)` adds `word` to the data structure, it can be matched later.
- `bool search(word)` returns `true` if there is any string in the data structure that matches `word` or `false` otherwise. `word` may contain dots `'.'` where dots can be matched with **any** letter.
constraints: word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters
word in search consists of '.' or lowercase English letters
There will be at most 2 dots in word for search queries when calling search
At most 10⁴ calls will be made to addWord and search
understanding: Build a dictionary where stored words are plain lowercase strings, but a query may contain '.' wildcards that each match any single letter. A query matches if SOME stored word fits the pattern exactly (same length, every non-dot character equal). The trie shares prefixes; the dot forces the search to explore multiple branches.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does a '.' match exactly one character, or zero-or-more?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Exactly one — like regex '.', not '*'. So the pattern and the matched word always have the same length. That's what keeps it a single-step branch rather than full regex DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the wildcard appear anywhere, including the first or last position?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A leading '.' just means the DFS branches over all children of the root on step 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could a query be all dots, like "...."?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that matches any stored word of that exact length. It's also the worst case: the DFS fans out to O(26^L). The constraint here caps dots at 2, keeping it tame.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If the pattern's path exists but no word ends there, is it a match?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Reaching the end of the pattern is necessary but not sufficient — the landing node must have isEnd = true, exactly like Implement Trie's search.

examples.explanation: No stored word is "pad" — the root has no 'p' child, so the DFS fails on the first character.
Exact path b→a→d exists and 'd' has isEnd = true. No wildcard, so it's a plain trie walk.
The '.' branches into root's children b, d, m. From 'b' the path a→d reaches a word end → return true (we stop at the first success).

approaches.name: Trie + DFS Backtracking on '.' (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the canonical solution. Frame it as 'a trie where search becomes a DFS so a dot can branch into every child'.

complexity.time: addWord O(L); search O(L) with no dots, up to O(26^d · L) with d dots
complexity.space: O(total characters) for the trie, O(L) recursion stack

hints: Store the words in a normal trie — addWord is just insert.
search a word without dots is a plain trie walk. Now: what do you do at a '.', where any letter is acceptable?
At a '.', you can't pick one child, so try them ALL — recurse into each child for the rest of the pattern and succeed if any branch matches.
approaches.complexityReasoning: addWord walks L characters, O(1) each → O(L). search follows one child per literal character; each '.' multiplies the branching by the number of children (≤26). With d dots the worst case is O(26^d · L), but with no dots it stays O(L). The trie stores the sum of all inserted characters; recursion depth is at most L.
approaches.explanation:
Reuse the Implement-Trie skeleton: nodes have a children map and an `isEnd` flag, and `addWord` is the unchanged insert. All the new work lives in `search`.

**Why search must become recursive.** Without wildcards, search is the same iterative walk as Implement Trie — follow one child per character, check isEnd at the end. The moment a `.` appears, the iterative walk breaks: you can no longer pick *the* child, because any of the (up to 26) children is a legal match. The natural way to 'try all options and accept if one works' is depth-first search with backtracking.

**Why a dot branches over every child.** A `.` means 'any single character'. So from the current node, *each* existing child is a candidate for that position. We recurse into every child with the rest of the pattern (index + 1) and return true if any of those sub-searches succeeds — that's the `any(dfs(child, i+1) ...)` line. A literal letter is the degenerate case: exactly one child is a candidate, so we recurse into just that one (or fail if it's missing).

**Why the base case checks isEnd, not just true.** When the pattern index reaches the word length, we've consumed the whole pattern. But matching the characters isn't enough — a stored *word* must actually end at this node. Returning `node.isEnd` (not `true`) is what stops `"ba"` from matching when only `"bad"` was inserted. This is the same isEnd discipline as Implement Trie, now inside a recursion.

**Why we pass node + index.** Carrying the current node and the position in the pattern (rather than slicing the string at each step) keeps each call O(1) extra work and avoids quadratic string copying. It also makes backtracking automatic: when a branch returns false, the recursion unwinds and the caller simply tries the next child.
approaches.insight: The literal-vs-dot distinction is the whole algorithm: a letter PRUNES the search to one child, a dot EXPANDS it to all children. Search cost is therefore driven entirely by how many dots the query has — pure-letter queries stay O(L), dotty queries fan out. This 'walk the trie, but branch and backtrack at choice points' move is exactly what Word Search II does on a grid.

java.explanation: Literal letter: prune to the one matching child, or fail if it's absent.

python.explanation: Whole pattern matched character-wise — check for a real word end next.
Reaching the end is necessary but not sufficient; is_end makes it an exact word match.
Wildcard — branch over all children rather than picking one.

python.line: return any(dfs(idx + 1, child) for child in node.children.values())
python.explanation: Short-circuits on the first matching branch via any(); no need to explore the rest.

python.line: return ch in node.children and dfs(idx + 1, node.children[ch])
python.explanation: Literal letter: only the one child is a candidate; missing child → False without recursing.

diagrams.title: Search recursion as a decision tree
diagrams.caption: A literal character takes the single-child edge; a dot fans out to all children and backtracks until one branch reaches an isEnd node.

edgeCases.behavior: Dot branches over root's children; only 'b' exists, b→a→d ends on isEnd → true. Confirms the dot tries existing children, not all 26 blindly.
Follow 'b', then two dots each branch over the single available child a→d, landing on isEnd → true.

pitfalls: Returning true (not node.isEnd) at the base case — lets a prefix like "ba" match when only "bad" was added.
On a dot, iterating all 26 array slots without the null check — you'd recurse into non-existent children and crash or waste work.
Slicing the word (word[1:]) on each recursion instead of passing an index — turns each call into O(L) string work, quadratic overall.

approaches.name: Bucket Words by Length + Linear Scan (Naive Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the quick first idea, then explain why it degrades when many words share a length — motivating the trie.

complexity.time: addWord O(L); search O(K · L) where K = words of that length

hints: A '.' matches any single character, so a candidate word must have the SAME length as the pattern.
Group stored words by length in a hash map: length → list of words.
search compares the pattern against every same-length word position-by-position, treating '.' as a wildcard. Simple, but it scans the whole bucket.
approaches.complexityReasoning: addWord appends to a list in O(L). search examines every word in the matching-length bucket and compares L characters each → O(K · L), where K can be large when many words share a length.
approaches.explanation:
Since `.` matches exactly one character, any matching word has the same length as the pattern. So bucket the words by length, and on search compare the pattern against each same-length word, treating `.` as 'always equal'.

**Why it's a reasonable first thought.** It directly exploits the same-length observation and needs no tree. For small dictionaries it's perfectly fast and trivially correct.

**Why it doesn't scale.** All the words of a given length sit in one bucket with no shared structure, so search must scan the entire bucket — O(K · L). With up to 10⁴ words, many sharing a length, repeated searches become a per-call linear scan. There's no prefix sharing and no early pruning: even a query that diverges on the first character still pays to start comparing every word.

**Why the trie wins.** The trie shares prefixes, so a literal character immediately prunes to one branch and a search that diverges early stops early. The bucket scan has no such pruning. Mention this baseline to show the same-length insight, then upgrade to the trie + DFS.
approaches.insight: Bucketing by length captures the 'dot matches one char' insight but throws away prefix structure, so it can never prune — every search rescans a whole bucket. The trie keeps the prefix structure, turning the scan into a guided DFS that abandons dead branches immediately.

pitfalls: Comparing words of different lengths — a '.' matches exactly one char, so only same-length words can match.
Forgetting the bucket may be absent (null) and dereferencing it.
Assuming this is 'good enough' — with many same-length words it becomes a per-query linear scan the trie avoids.

commonMistakes: Returning true at the end of the pattern instead of node.isEnd — a prefix wrongly matches.
Trying to handle '.' iteratively (picking one child) instead of branching into all children with DFS.
Recursing into children without a null/existence check on a dot, exploring edges that don't exist.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Base case returns true instead of isEnd
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the pattern is consumed, the path's characters all matched — but a stored WORD must actually end at this node. Returning true lets a strict prefix match: search("ba") would return true after only "bad" was added.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Branching into non-existent children on a dot
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Iterating a fixed 26-slot array and recursing without the null check explores edges that don't exist — at best wasted work, at worst a NullPointerException one level down.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Slicing the pattern each recursion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Calling dfs(word[1:], node) copies the suffix on every level, turning an O(L) search into O(L²) and allocating garbage. Pass an index instead.

followupVariations.hint: Adds '*' (zero-or-more), which breaks the same-length invariant and needs DP, not a single-step branch.

followupVariations.title: Wildcard Matching
followupVariations.hint: '?' is this problem's '.', but '*' matches any sequence — again DP territory.

patternNote: Canonical Trie + DFS backtracking. Recognise it when an exact-match dictionary gains single-character wildcards: literals prune to one child, dots fan out to all. The same 'walk a trie but branch at choice points' shape powers Word Search II.
